what: Human approval is a pause point in an agent: before a risky or irreversible tool call (publish, send, delete, spend money), the agent stops, shows a person what it plans to do, and only continues once they approve.
like: Like a junior writer who drafts the newsletter but waits for the editor to sign it off before it goes to print.
why: Stops costly mistakes the model cannot undo - a wrong email, a deleted table, a refund
Keeps people accountable: every approval says who decided, what and when
Lets you ship agents earlier, then loosen the gate as trust and evals grow

nodes.t: Durable wait|state saved, can pause days

steps.d: The agent drafts a blog post and asks to call publish_post. Nothing has happened yet - it is only a proposal with arguments.
Code, not the model, checks a risk tier. Read-only or reversible calls (search, save draft) run straight away. Publish, send, delete and spend need a person.
The run pauses durably: LangGraph interrupt() saves state through a checkpointer, or a Temporal workflow waits for a signal. Workers can restart; the run waits safely.
The marketer sees exactly what will happen: the rendered post, a diff against the last version, the target channel. They approve, edit the arguments, or reject with a note.
Every wait has a deadline. If nobody answers, notify a backup approver, then auto-reject safely. Never auto-approve on timeout.
The decision resumes the run with the approved arguments, the tool runs once, and the audit log stores who approved what, when and why.

choices.d: Sort every tool: auto (read-only, reversible), notify (runs, then tells someone), approve (publish, send, delete, spend). Keep the approve list short so each request deserves attention.
Durable engine: LangGraph interrupt with a database checkpointer, or Temporal signals. Never an in-memory loop or open HTTP request - a deploy would lose the pending approval.
A rendered preview plus a diff, the exact tool arguments, the agent's reason and sources. Let the reviewer edit arguments, not only click yes or no.
Pick a deadline per tier, a backup approver to escalate to, and a safe default (reject or keep as draft). Signals that arrive after the timeout must be ignored cleanly.
Check the approver's role in code, and for big spends require two people. The agent's own output must never count as an approval.

instead.why: Automatic filters catch known bad content without a person in the loop
Let the agent act freely inside an isolated box that cannot hurt anything
A second model grades outputs at scale; humans review only the low scores
Narrow, least-privilege tools remove the risky action in the first place

breaks.d: Too many requests, so reviewers click approve without reading.
breaks.see: Median review time drops to seconds; approve rate near 100%
breaks.fix: Auto-allow low-risk tiers, batch similar items, show only what changed

breaks.d: On resume LangGraph re-runs the node from its start, so code before the interrupt repeats.
breaks.see: Duplicate emails or posts after an approval
breaks.fix: Put the interrupt first in the node and side effects after it; make tools idempotent

breaks.d: The wait lived in memory and a deploy restarted the worker.
breaks.see: Requests stuck with no reviewer task, or agents that never resume
breaks.fix: Use a durable checkpointer or workflow engine; keep thread_id with the request

breaks.d: The reviewer approves one thing and the agent runs slightly different arguments.
breaks.see: Audit log arguments do not match what was shown
breaks.fix: Approve a hash of the exact arguments; run only those, re-ask on any change

breaks.d: Nobody owns the queue and there is no deadline.
breaks.see: Growing age of the oldest pending request
breaks.fix: Timeouts per tier, escalation to a backup, safe auto-reject

say: I give the agent free use of read-only and reversible tools, and a policy check in code puts publish, send, delete and spend behind a human approval gate.
The pause is durable - LangGraph interrupt with a Postgres checkpointer, or a Temporal workflow waiting on a signal with a timeout - so a deploy never loses a pending approval.
The reviewer sees a preview and a diff of the exact arguments, can edit or reject, and the tool runs only with what was approved; every decision lands in an audit log.
I watch approve rate and review time to spot approval fatigue, and as evals improve I move tools down a risk tier.

followups.q: Why not let the model decide when to ask for approval?
followups.a: The model can be wrong or prompt-injected. OWASP's excessive agency guidance says enforce authorisation in downstream code, so the gate is a fixed policy on the tool, not a choice the model makes.

followups.q: How do you stop approval fatigue?
followups.a: Risk tiers so only high-impact calls reach a person, batching similar requests, a clear diff instead of a wall of text, and tracking approve rate and time per review. If everything is approved, the gate is in the wrong place.

followups.q: What happens if the approver never answers?
followups.a: Each wait has a timeout. Escalate to a backup approver, then reject safely or keep the item as a draft. Ignore approvals that arrive after the timeout fired.

followups.q: How do you scale review for thousands of items?
followups.a: Auto-approve what passes guardrails and an LLM judge, sample a small share for human review, and send only low-confidence or high-risk items to the queue.

today: LangGraph made interrupt() the recommended way to pause for a human as of v1.0, and OWASP's 2025 LLM Top 10 lists human approval of high-impact actions as a core fix for excessive agency.

check.q: An agent wants to publish a post and to search the web. Which needs approval?
check.why: Publishing is public and hard to undo; read-only search is safe to auto-allow.

check.q: Nobody answers an approval within the deadline. The safest default?
check.a: Escalate, then reject or keep as draft
check.why: A timeout should fail safe. Auto-approving would make the gate pointless.

check.q: Why must the pause be stored durably?
check.a: So a restart or deploy does not lose the pending approval
d: So the reviewer can skip the preview
Because LLMs need disk to think
check.why: Approvals can take hours or days; a checkpointer or workflow engine keeps the state safe.

check.q: Reviewers approve almost everything in two seconds. What is happening?
check.why: Too many low-risk requests. Auto-allow safe tiers so each request deserves real attention.
